extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of poetry, drama, and literary criticism (poets, dramatists, critics, scholars)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating tragic drama and poetic diction: principles of plot unity, chorus integration, diction/thought, metaphor, and word-formation as set out in Aristotle's Poetics (with editorial notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine poetic merits
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should endeavour, if possible, to combine all poetic merits; or failing that, the greatest number and those the most important; the more so, in face of the cavilling criticism of the day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a tragedy that attains multiple lines of excellence (plot, character, diction, thought, spectacle, chorus). If unable to achieve all, prioritise the greatest number and most important merits so the work can withstand contemporary critical demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot as the test of sameness or difference
rubrics_metrics.description: In speaking of a tragedy as the same or different, the best test to take is the plot. Identity exists where the Complication and Unravelling are the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate works by comparing their central complication and its resolution. Two works are ‘the same’ if they share the same knot (complication) and unravelling (denouement); otherwise they differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master both complication (knot-tying) and unraveling
rubrics_metrics.description: Many poets tie the knot well, but unravel it ill. Both arts, however, should always be mastered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good dramatist must be skilled at constructing the central complication and at executing a satisfying, coherent unravelling; weakness in either undermines the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making a tragedy into an Epic structure (no multiplicity of plots)
rubrics_metrics.description: Again, the poet should remember what has been often said, and not make a Tragedy into an Epic structure. By an Epic structure I mean one with a multiplicity of plots: as if, for instance, you were to make a tragedy out of the entire story of the Iliad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a single coherent portion of a larger tale rather than dramatizing an entire epic narrative. Anti-patterns: attempting to stage entire epics (Fall of Troy, whole Niobe story) leads to failure or poor success on stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reversals of action to produce satisfying tragic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: In his Reversals of the Action ... he shows a marvellous skill in the effort to hit the popular taste—to produce a tragic effect that satisfies the moral sense. This effect is produced when the clever rogue, like Sisyphus, is outwitted, or the brave villain defeated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reversals should be crafted to surprise yet feel morally and probabilistically acceptable (Agathon's notion that 'many things should happen contrary to probability'). Successful reversals align audience sympathy and moral satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus as an integral actor
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus too should be regarded as one of the actors; it should be an integral part of the whole, and share in the action, in the manner not of Euripides but of Sophocles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the choral songs and interventions contribute to the subject and action rather than serve as mere interludes. Anti-pattern: choral songs that pertain as little to the piece as to any other tragedy (mere interludes) — akin to transferring a speech or whole act between plays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought: include proof/refutation and excite feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Thought is included every effect which has to be produced by speech; in particular,—proof and refutation; the excitation of the feelings, such as pity, fear, anger, and the like; the suggestion of importance or its opposite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design speeches to achieve rhetorical aims (argument, persuasion, emotional arousal). Judge thought by whether speeches produce intended effects (pity, fear, anger, sense of importance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat dramatic incidents and speeches from same points of view; incidents should speak for themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: The dramatic incidents must be treated from the same points of view as the dramatic speeches, when the object is to evoke the sense of pity, fear, importance, or probability. The only difference is, that the incidents should speak for themselves without verbal exposition; while the effects aimed at in a speech should be produced by the speaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let actions on stage convey their own meaning rather than relying on explanatory speeches; use speeches where the speaker must generate the effect. Avoid redundant verbal exposition that simply restates what incidents already show.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of expression (declamation) awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: One branch of the inquiry treats of the Modes of Expression. ... It includes, for instance,—what is a command, a prayer, a narrative, a threat, a question, an answer, and so forth. To know or not to know these things involves no serious censure upon the poet’s art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of speech-types and their performative effect (command vs. prayer vs. narrative). This belongs more to the art of declamation/performer-training than to poetry per se, but influences diction and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand language constituents for style and metre
rubrics_metrics.description: Language in general includes the following parts: the Letter, the Syllable, the Connecting word, the Noun, the Verb, the Inflexion or Case, the Proposition or Phrase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical knowledge of letters, syllables, connecting words, inflexions, and phrases matters for metre, diction, and clarity. Consider syllable formation (mute+vowel etc.) when composing verse and assessing rhythm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise and use appropriate word-types
rubrics_metrics.description: Every word is either current, or strange, or metaphorical, or ornamental, or newly-coined, or lengthened, or contracted; or altered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify words and choose types to suit tone and genre. Current/proper words give clarity; strange/rare/metaphorical/ornamental words raise diction. Use invention (neologisms), lengthening, contraction, and alteration judiciously for effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphor: types and correct application
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphor is the application of an alien name by transference either from genus to species, or from species to genus, or from species to species, or by analogy, that is, proportion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ metaphors by genus↔species or by proportion (analogy). You may qualify metaphors by adding the term to which the proper word is relative. Even when one term lacks a specific name, metaphor by proportion can be effective. Command of metaphor is a mark of genius; it requires an eye for resemblances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use lengthening/contracting/alteration to gain distinction (with moderation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing contributes more to produce a clearness of diction that is remote from commonness than the lengthening, contraction, and alteration of words. For by deviating in exceptional cases from the normal idiom, the language will gain distinction; while, at the same time, the partial conformity with usage will give perspicuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these licenses to create distinction while retaining overall intelligibility. Critics who blanketly censure such licenses are mistaken, but obtrusive or excessive use becomes grotesque.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfection of style: clear without being mean (balance current and unusual)
rubrics_metrics.description: The perfection of style is to be clear without being mean. The clearest style is that which uses only current or proper words; at the same time it is mean. ... A diction wholly composed of such words is either a riddle or a jargon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance ordinary (current) words for clarity with some rare, metaphorical, or ornamental terms to avoid banality. Too many metaphors make a riddle; too many strange words make a jargon. An infusion of unusual elements is necessary to elevate style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in use of figurative and unusual diction
rubrics_metrics.description: To employ such license at all obtrusively is, no doubt, grotesque; but in any mode of poetic diction there must be moderation. Even metaphors, strange (or rare) words, or any similar forms of speech, would produce the like effect if used without propriety, and with the express purpose of being ludicrous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid conspicuous, gratuitous, or excessive use of rare words and metaphors. Use unusual diction only where it fits tone and effect; otherwise it risks ridicule or grotesqueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-appropriate diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the various kinds of words, the compound are best adapted to dithyrambs, rare words to heroic poetry, metaphors to iambic. In heroic poetry, indeed, all these varieties are serviceable. But in iambic verse, which reproduces, as far as may be, familiar speech, the most appropriate words are those which are found even in prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match word-formation and diction to the specific poetic genre: use compounds in dithyrambs; rare/ornamental words in heroic poetry; metaphors and everyday prose-like words in iambic. Choose the vocabulary set that best serves the meter and audience expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-action unity for narrative imitation in single metre
rubrics_metrics.description: As to that poetic imitation which is narrative in form and employs a single metre, the plot manifestly ought, as in a tragedy, to be constructed on dramatic principles. It should have for its subject a single action, whole and complete, with a beginning, a middle, and an end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing narrative poems in a single metre (i.e., narrative-dramatic imitation), enforce unity of action: one coherent action with clear beginning, middle, and end. Avoid episodic/fragmented chronicle structures.
